keyVerseText: And it came to pass, when he made mention of the ark of God, that he fell from off the seat backward by the side of the gate, and his neck brake, and he died: for he was an old man, and heavy. And he had judged Israel forty years.
rootMeaning: The root of מִפְרֶקֶת (miphreqeth) comes from the Hebrew verb פָּרַק (pâraq), which primarily means to break off, tear apart, or rend. This root conveys a sense of separation or breaking away, which enriches the basic meaning of 'neck' by emphasizing the neck as the joint or fracture point connecting the head to the body. Thus, the literal sense involves a vulnerable juncture capable of being broken or separated, not merely a physical part but a critical point of connection and potential fracture.
usageInScripture: The term מִפְרֶקֶת appears only once in Scripture, specifically in 1 Samuel 4:18, where it is translated as 'and his neck.' This singular occurrence shows a precise and literal use, referring to the physical neck as the vulnerable joint that breaks. The consistent translation as 'neck' underscores the word's straightforward anatomical meaning without figurative extension in the biblical text.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מִפְרֶקֶת as the neck—the fragile joint linking head and body—carries profound theological symbolism. It highlights human vulnerability and the reality of mortality, reminding believers of the fragility of life under the sovereignty of God. The neck as a point of potential breaking can also symbolize the breaking of human pride or the submission of the whole person (body) to the head, which in Christian faith is Christ. Therefore, this word deepens our appreciation of human dependence on God’s sustaining power and the hope of redemption from brokenness through Christ.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Samuel 4:18, the phrase 'and his neck brake, and he died' uses מִפְרֶקֶת to describe the fatal injury of Eli. This word vividly conveys the physical reality of his death by highlighting the breaking of the neck as the cause. It emphasizes the sudden and irreversible nature of his demise, reinforcing the gravity of the moment when the ark of God was mentioned, and symbolizing the collapse of an era in Israel’s history.
